abstract: Abstract Summary The inference of kinase activity from phosphoproteomics data can point to causal mechanisms driving signalling processes and potential drug targets. Identifying the kinases whose change in activity explains the observed phosphorylation profiles, however, remains challenging, and constrained by the manually curated knowledge of kinase–substrate associations. Recently, experimentally determined substrate sequence specificities of human kinases have become available, but robust methods to exploit this new data for kinase activity inference are still missing. We present PhosX, a method to estimate differential kinase activity from phosphoproteomics data that combines state-of-the-art statistics in enrichment analysis with kinases’ substrate sequence specificity information. Using a large phosphoproteomics dataset with known differentially regulated kinases we show that our method identifies upregulated and downregulated kinases by only relying on the input phosphopeptides’ sequences and intensity changes. We find that PhosX outperforms the currently available approach for the same task, and performs better or similarly to state-of-the-art methods that rely on previously known kinase–substrate associations. We therefore recommend its use for data-driven kinase activity inference. Availability and implementation PhosX is implemented in Python, open-source under the Apache-2.0 licence, and distributed on the Python Package Index. The code is available on GitHub ( https://github.com/alussana/phosx ).

1 Introduction
Kinases are major drivers of intracellular signalling, their activity contributing to virtually all biological processes. As they are often deregulated in disease, they are prevalent targets of approved drugs (
Bhullar
et al.
2018
). Current phosphoproteomics techniques enable the quantification of thousands of phosphosites, allowing for unbiased assessments of intracellular signalling states. There are multiple methods that infer kinase activities from this data based on previously known kinase–substrate relationships, often combining other information such as local networks, structure and other features (
Müller-Dott
et al.
2024
). However, only a small fraction of discovered human phosphosites (
Hornbeck
et al.
2015
) have at least one known upstream kinase (
Needham
et al.
2019
), posing a challenge to the comprehensive estimation of kinase activity from phosphoproteomics data. At the same time, 150 human kinases have no known substrate, despite all of them likely being essential for normal human function (
Meehan
et al.
2017
). Recently, an atlas of substrate sequence specificity for 303 human Serine/Threonine kinases and 78 human Tyrosine kinases has been built for the first time, by employing a cell-free method known as positional scanning peptide assay (PSPA) (
Johnson
et al.
2023
,
Yaron-Barir
et al.
2024
). This resource can be used to link kinases to their potential target phosphosites in a data-driven manner opening the door to the accurate inference of all Ser/Thr and Tyr kinase activities, regardless of the prior knowledge associated with them, and considering full phosphoproteomics datasets as opposed to the limited number of phosphosites with upstream kinase annotations. It also allows phospho-priming to be systematically taken into account when evaluating the affinity of a kinase for a given substrate. We anticipate data-driven differential kinase activity inference to become a powerful tool in cell signalling research and drug discovery, but robust and benchmarked computational methods to perform this task are still missing. To address this need we developed PhosX, a software package to perform differential kinase activity inference from phosphoproteomics experiments using substrate sequence specificity data and state-of-the art statistics in enrichment analysis. We benchmarked its performance in recovering expected changes in kinase activity and we show that it outperforms the currently proposed method to perform the same task while requiring fewer arbitrary parameters, as well as commonly used methods that use previously known kinase–substrate associations.

3 Results
We developed PhosX, a software package to infer differential kinase activities from phosphoproteomics data that does not require any prior knowledge database of kinase-phosphosite associations. PhosX assigns the phosphopeptides detected in an experiment to potential upstream kinases based on their substrate sequence specificity, which has been recently determined experimentally in the form of Position-Specific Scoring Matrices (PSSMs) (
Johnson
et al.
2023
) (
Yaron-Barir
et al.
2024
); it then tests the enrichment of a kinase’s potential substrates in the extremes of the distribution of phosphopeptide intensity changes, using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov-like statistic analogous to the one implemented in the popular Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) method (
Subramanian
et al.
2005
) (
Fig. 1A
). PhosX can therefore be used to link observed changes in phosphorylation profiles to potential causal kinases, taking into consideration all detected phosphosites regardless of the amount of prior knowledge, if any, available for any specific phosphosite. PhosX is implemented in Python, can be easily installed from the Python Package Index, and can optionally take advantage of multiple cores to parallelize the computation.

To evaluate the biological relevance of the kinase activity scores computed with PhosX, we used a benchmark dataset of 103 perturbation experiments for which phosphosite log fold changes are publicly available (
Hernandez-Armenta
et al.
2017
). Each experiment is associated with kinases that are expected to be up- or down-regulated due to the nature of the perturbation (
Hernandez-Armenta
et al.
2017
). Overall, our benchmark comprises data for 28 unique kinases, including 173 ‘ground truth’ examples of kinase activities among which 100 are upregulated and 73 downregulated. In our assessment we included five other methods with complementary characteristics: Kinex (
Valeanu
et al.
2023
), which to our knowledge is the only currently available method inferring potential kinase-phosphosite interactions based on PSSM scores, but, differently from PhosX, it uses the Fisher’s exact test to predict kinase activity changes; and GSEApy (
Fang
et al.
2023
), which, used in conjunction with the PhosphositePlus database (
Hornbeck
et al.
2015
), implements the same statistic as PhosX, but only considers known kinase-phosphosite interactions curated from the literature. The remaining methods [
z
-score (
Ilmaz
et al.
2021
), PTM-Sea (
Krug
et al.
2019
) and KSTAR (
Crowl
et al.
2022
)] are commonly used and well-performing methods for this task (
Müller-Dott
et al.
2024
). To ensure a fair comparison across methods we aimed to compare their performance on identifying kinase activities for the same set of kinases. As the universal overlap of the possible kinase activity inferences per method was too small, we performed the evaluation in a pairwise fashion, comparing PhosX to each method independently.
First, the linear separation based on the kinase activity score between positively and negatively regulated kinases in the ground-truth set was marginally greater for PhosX compared to GSEApy and KSTAR, and clearly greater compared to the
z
-score, Kinex and PTM-SEA, both when considering the area under the Receiving Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) (
Supplementary Fig. S1
) and the area under the Precision–Recall curve (AUPR) (
Fig. 1B
). This indicates the ability of PhosX to distinguish up- from down-regulation in the set of known regulated kinases. We then evaluated the normalized rank in which the ‘true’ kinase appears in the activity score distribution from PhosX and the methods to which we compared it and found that PhosX generally ranked these higher, with the exception of KSTAR and GSEApy, which performed very similarly (
Fig. 1C
). The performance of PhosX on these metrics was independent of the number of top kinase matches we considered for each phosphosite (
Supplementary Fig. S2
). Next, we considered the task of distinguishing known regulated kinases from an equally sized set of examples where the kinases are not expected to be affected by the perturbations. We built such a negative set by randomly drawing kinase-experiment pairs, and repeated the evaluation 100 times, each time with a different random negative set, to account for technical variability. While we expect the presence of false negatives in this classification task, we observed favourable AUROC and AUPR for PhosX compared to all the other methods, except for GSEApy which performed marginally better on identifying down regulated kinases (
Fig. 1D
and
Supplementary Fig. S3
). We also computed the fraction of upregulated and downregulated ground-truth examples found in the respective extremes of the kinase activity score distribution according to each method. This metric provides a lower bound on the expected probability of discovering an upregulated or downregulated kinase among the ones inferred to be most affected by the perturbations. We defined such extremes as the top-5 and bottom-5 percentiles of activity score, and found that PhosX recovered substantially more kinases among the ones expected to be strongly regulated than the other methods with the exception of KSTAR which recovered marginally more downregulated kinases and similar upregulated ones (
Fig. 1E
and
F
,
Supplementary Fig. S4
). Conversely, Kinex had the worst performance in this task, with only rare instances of known regulated kinases being found at the extremes of the activity score distribution (
Supplementary Fig. S5
), and we observed this being the case independently from the choice of log fold change threshold (
Supplementary Fig. S6
).
4 Discussion and future work
We present PhosX, a tool to infer kinase activities from phosphoproteomics datasets based on the data and PSSM-based kinase substrate specificities alone. Despite our benchmarking being based on highly studied kinases with several known substrates, PhosX still outperformed most methods it was compared to, with GSEApy which uses a similar statistic and KSTAR performing similarly, highlighting the power of using the unbiased PSSMs for this task and implying the suitability of PhosX for inferring activities also for understudied kinases. Similarly, despite using the same PSSMs as a basis, PhosX outperformed Kinex, in particular in identifying the correct regulated kinases in the extreme 5th percentiles than both methods, confirming the power of the rank sum statistic for this task (
Hernandez-Armenta
et al.
2017
,
Müller-Dott
et al.
2024
). PhosX performed particularly well, when identifying upregulated kinases, which is perhaps a consequence of the fact that upregulated kinases would lead to a more clear kinase specificity signal in peptides of increasing abundance, whereas phosphopeptides of decreasing abundance may be a result of different types of regulation, such as dephosphorylation, degradation and others. The statistical framework implemented in PhosX may be used together with any scoring function that assigns kinases to target phosphosites. While we can conclude that PSSM scores are useful for this purpose, substrate sequence specificity is not the only driver of kinase-phosphosite interactions. The presence of adaptor proteins, subcellular localization, post-translational modifications, kinase expression, etc., are all factors that determine whether the phosphorylation of a target by a given kinase is mechanistically possible, but are not taken into account by the PSSM model alone. Furthermore, PSSMs of evolutionarily related kinases tend to be similar, leading to correlations in estimated kinase activities which may not be true. These limitations might be greatly alleviated by introducing better scoring functions, e.g. using machine learning classifiers that consider features beyond substrate specificity, or taking into consideration the local functional neighbourhood of the kinase (
Linding
et al.
2008
,
Ilmaz
et al.
2021
). Phosphoproteomics readouts result from the combined effect of the activity of all kinases and phosphatases, while the approach presented here treats kinases independently. We hypothesize that statistical modelling approaches that allow us to infer the activity of every kinase in combination with all the others may be worth exploring in future research.
